USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current tariff posture without new escalation or concession. The existing $250B tariff coverage and the scheduled January 1 rise from 10% to 25% on List 3 already exert significant leverage. Allow that pressure to work while keeping the door open for talks. Do not announce new tariffs before the midterms, but do not roll anything back either — the strategic position favors the US.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of -0.3 reflects a position of relative US advantage. China is running out of retaliatory capacity: its latest response covered only $60B of US goods at reduced rates of 5-10%, down from the 25% matching it used on earlier rounds (CNN, Sept 19). Capital Economics noted China 'has been unable to match the US dollar-for-dollar.' Meanwhile the US still has a $267B tariff threat in reserve that would cover virtually all remaining Chinese exports. US macro data shows an economy absorbing the trade shock well: consumer sentiment at 100.1 (UMich Sept 2018), industrial production at 104.1 (Aug 2018), and unemployment near historic lows. The dollar has strengthened ~5.5% over six months (DTWEXBGS), reflecting capital flows into US assets.

However, the position is not costless. Soybean farmers face devastating losses — prices down ~$1.90/bu vs Brazilian competitors, Chinese orders down 80% year-over-year (farmdoc daily, Sept 10). The USDA's $12B aid package (announced Aug 27) is a stopgap, not a solution, and farm-state senators are restless ahead of November midterms. Corporate bond spreads (Baa) have widened ~31bp to 4.9%, suggesting some credit stress.

The action score of 0.0 (hold) is justified by several factors: (1) List 3 just took effect on Sept 24 — its full impact hasn't been felt yet, and adding more tariffs now would increase uncertainty without clear strategic gain; (2) the scheduled Jan 1 step-up to 25% is a built-in escalation lever that can be used as a negotiating deadline; (3) China has not yet canceled trade talks entirely — Foreign Ministry spokesman Geng Shuang said the new tariffs 'brought uncertainty' but stopped short of pulling out (Politico, Sept 18); Kudlow publicly invited renewed talks on Sept 12; (4) midterms are 5 weeks away, and further escalation risks alienating farm-state voters without proportionate gain; (5) as Arthur Kroeber of Gavekal noted, the principal objective may be 'to force US multinational companies to pull back their investments in China' — that structural shift is already underway and doesn't require additional tariff rounds. The right play is strategic patience: hold what we have, let the Jan 1 deadline create pressure, and see if Beijing sends Liu He to Washington.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should pursue calibrated negotiation without making preemptive concessions, while continuing to deploy domestic stimulus to offset tariff damage. Retaliate symmetrically on any further escalation, but signal willingness to talk — the asymmetry of the trade relationship means time is not on China's side, and the List 3 escalation to 25% in January 2019 would be significantly more damaging than the current 10%. Avoid further yuan depreciation beyond what has already occurred to prevent capital flight and accusations of manipulation.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.65 reflects the severe and escalating nature of the trade war as of September 27, 2018. The US has now imposed tariffs on approximately $250 billion of Chinese imports across three lists (timeline entry 2018-09-24: List 3 took effect at 10%, combined Section 301 coverage ~$250B), and Trump has explicitly threatened to tariff ALL remaining Chinese imports (~$267B more) if China retaliates (timeline entry 2018-06-18). Economists estimate tariffs could reduce Chinese GDP growth by 0.5-0.6 percentage points in 2019 if List 3 rises to 25% as scheduled (CNBC, Sept 19, 2018). The Caixin PMI fell to a 14-month low of 50.6 in August with export orders declining for five consecutive months (CNBC, Sept 3, 2018), and Premier Li Keqiang acknowledged 'greater difficulties in keeping stable performance of the Chinese economy' (CNBC, Sept 19). The yuan has depreciated ~7% against the dollar since April, providing some offset but raising capital flight risks — the PBOC reintroduced the counter-cyclical factor in late August to arrest the decline (Reuters, Sept 3). China's retaliatory capacity is constrained by the trade asymmetry: China exports ~4x as much to the US as it imports, meaning matching retaliation has a ceiling. Meanwhile, the US economy shows remarkable strength — consumer sentiment at 100.1, industrial production rising, dollar appreciating ~5.5% — meaning the US can absorb trade war pain more easily.

The action score of -0.15 (mild negotiate) reflects a strategic calculus: China cannot win an escalation spiral given the asymmetry, but neither should it capitulate. The List 3 tariff is only at 10% now, not 25% — there is a window before January 2019 to explore terms. China should leverage its remaining tools (stimulus, selective retaliation, multilateral positioning as defender of WTO rules) while engaging diplomatically. Domestically, the RRR cuts and infrastructure spending already underway should be accelerated. The goal is to buy time and reach a framework that avoids the 25% escalation without conceding structural issues (Made in China 2025, state subsidies) that would undermine long-term strategic objectives.
